Emily signed up for the Ultragenyx trial and Warren volunteered for the Vivet trial. In our Winter 2023 newsletter we introduced them to the WD community. Emily received her diagnosis five years before on her 35th birthday, while Warren was diagnosed in 1980 at age seven. Emily is a wife and mom to a four-year-old son and works as a school secretary. Warren is a husband and dad to an 11-year-old daughter and had to give up his job as a preacher due to WD complications. The story of their patient experience left off with Emily and Warren facing the decision of whether or not to participate in a trial designed to determine if gene therapy in WD patients is safe, and works. Read More #### Important Update on UX701 Gene Therapy: On November 3, 2026, Ultragenyx announced that it is discontinuing development of UX701, an investigational gene therapy for Wilson disease, after clinical trial results did not demonstrate sufficient effectiveness to advance to Phase 3. We recognize that this news is disappointing for the Wilson disease community. Below is a letter from the Ultragenyx team explaining the decision, what it means for clinical trial participants, and the next steps. November 3, 2026 Dear Wilson Disease Community, The Ultragenyx team is reaching out with an important update to meet your request for ongoing updates about UX701, our investigational gene therapy for the potential treatment of Wilson disease. Ultragenyx has made the difficult decision to discontinue development of UX701 based on preliminary efficacy data from Phase 1/2 that have not demonstrated sufficient efficacy to move the program into Phase 3. Patients who received UX701 as part of the Cyprus2+ clinical study will continue to receive long-term safety monitoring. No new patients will receive UX701. We recognize this news is disappointing for the Wilson disease community. We are extremely grateful to the patients and families who participated in the Phase 1/2 study and the investigators who care for them. Additional information, including what happens next, are below. Preliminary Phase 1/2 results and rationale for discontinuing development of UX701 program: • The Phase 1/2 study enrolled 20 patients into four sequential dosing cohorts with the goal of identifying a dose with an appropriate safety and efficacy profile for further investigation in a pivotal phase 3 study. All patients in the Phase 1/2 study have now been followed for at least 52 weeks. • The decision was made to discontinue development of UX701 due to lack of efficacy. While some patients in several dose groups showed improvements in copper-based biomarkers, and several of them were able to discontinue standard of care medications and maintain acceptable copper levels for several years, these effects were inconsistent across dose cohorts. The highest dose group did not show a substantial improvement in biomarkers or efficacy compared to prior cohorts. • The decision to discontinue development was not made for safety reasons. Up until now, UX701 was well tolerated and has had an acceptable safety profile to date, including in the highest dose group and in participants who received the revised immunomodulation regimen. What happens next: • Patients who have received UX701 will continue to be monitored for long-term safety. Individual participants and their families will be contacted directly by their PI about specific next steps. • We are committed to sharing the full study results to help inform future learnings for the field. We plan to publish a manuscript and present the results at a scientific congress in 2027. We express our deep appreciation to the patients, families, investigators, study site staff, CRO partners, and the Wilson disease patient community for their support and contributions to this program. Individuals participating in the Cyprus2+ study should direct questions to their study site. Community members can direct questions to patientinquiry@ultragenyx.com. Sincerely, Andrew Grimm on behalf of the UX701 Team ## Gene Therapy Gene therapy is a technique designed to treat or prevent disease.
